newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Rate fears cause losses for dlr, Euro stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rate fears cause losses for dlr, Euro stocks.

text.p: European markets ended trade on Tuesday showing big losses for the dollar and stocks but with their attention firmly riveted on a meeting of U.S. central bankers who are deciding interest rates.

All eyes were focused on the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, and markets were almost evenly split on the prospects of a 25-basis-point interest rate rise in the power-house U.S. economy. A decision was not expected before 1815 GMT.

Shares in London, Paris , Frankfurt and Wall Street were all showing losses of about one percent in the countdown to the rates decision, with investors fretting that higher rates would hit profit margins.

At the same time, the dollar struggled to regain its poise after dropping to a five-month low of 111.98 yen, fighting uncertainty over U.S. interest rate policy and speculation about higher Japanese rates.
Traders said that at the moment, the mood seemed to be one of cashing in on any signs of dollar recovery.

In a volatile trading session on foreign exchanges, dealers began the day by unloading dollars because of worries that Japan might increase rates, making dollar-denominated assets less attractive to investors.
They drove the dollar down by nearly four yen after reports that a committee of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Partly (LDP) was considering asking for higher discount rates from the Bank of Japan.

But the currency later bounced back by nearly two yen and stood above 113 yen in late afternoon trade after Japanese officials warned the yen's rise had been too rapid and a Japanese rate rise was not likely soon.
"The dollar has recovered after Sakakibara (Eisuke) said the yen's rise had been too rapid," said Alessandra Stagliano, economist at Daiwa Europe.

Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, and known as "Mr Yen" for his influence over markets, said the pace of the yen's strengthening against the dollar was too rapid and that volatility was undesirable.
Despite the reassurances from Tokyo, the dollar remained well below the levels seen in late Europe on Monday. Against the mark, it was also down nearly two pfennigs
Currency traders -- unlike their equity colleagues-- detected a shift of mood away from Washington's commitment to a strong dollar before the meeting of the FOMC.

They cited comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin as evidence of Washington's change in tune. Rubin said the U.S. policy on the dollar remained unchanged -- but did not explicitly repeat his past support for a strong dollar.
The dollar has been spiralling downward since hitting a 56-month peak of 127.47 on May 1.
The uncertainty over U.S. rates went the other way in European bourses where the fear was that rates would go up and this cast a cloud over markets. A poor start in Wall Street added to the gloom.

Frankfurt suffered the most, with floor trade ending down 1.7 percent as the weaker dollar also hit exporting sectors. Many investors took up defensive positions before the FOMC but some dealers said the market was heading down, rate rise or not.
"After the price advances of recent weeks, there is clearly a lack of new positive impetus," Trinkhaus Capital Management said, summing up the mood of some market players .
Paris ended with losses of 1.2 percent, with the market divided over whether there would be no-change or a quarter percentage point rise in U.S. interest rates.

"We're coming up to a couple of key events -- the FOMC meeting, the French (parliamentary) election -- and the market's at record highs. It's normal to correct," one trader said. The CAC index rose 5.71 percent last week.
London also ended well down for the second day running amid worries about higher interest rates in Britain as well as on the other side of the Atlantic.
The FTSE 100 closed, which dropped nearly 50 points on Monday, ended 37.7 points down at 4,607.5.

"We've had a classic day of uncertainties. In this case it's about interest rates," the head of trading at a major brokerage said. "It's the fear of the unknown not the fact that has done the damage today."

Worries about the higher cost of borrowing in Britain are also expected to surface in coming weeks as investors await the new Labour government's first budget, which could take place as early as next month.
CLOSING STOCK PRICES
London's FTSE 100 ended down 37.7 points at 4,607.5.
The Paris CAC-40 index finished down 33.17 points at 2,751.17.
Frankfurt's DAX index closed down 61.12 points at 3,543.43.
CURRENCIES
The dollar stood at 1.6953 marks and 113.80 yen compared with 1.7105 marks and 116.09 yen in late European trade on Monday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Palladium ended at $178.25 an ounce, up $5.25 after the highest fix since 1989. Gold ended at $342.75 ounce, compared with Monday's close in London of $341.25. Silver was at $4.71 up two cents.
